text: Scaling a growth team used to meet headcount. Now a team of one can run the same experiment program that used to take a team of five. And a team of five could run the same experiment program that used to take a team of 20. Welcome to the AI world. Team of one, you are a strategist, an executor and a leader, and your agents are their team. Team of five, you are their player coach, and every direct report runs agents on their own. Now the fork. Budges show up for the first hire, and the classic move is to list the work that you hate so you can pass it on to a junior. But that buys you zero leverage, zero. The better move. List the most impactful work, the work that moves the business towards its growth goals. Then figure out how someone could spend their time on exactly that. Team of one, that list goes to the agents, or you stop doing it. Variant copy for the landing page, onboarding variants, their weekly funnel readout, session recorder review, churn flags, failed payment retries. Team of five, every report builds that list for their slice of the funnel, and the first human hire goes into the highest impact work, not the leftovers. So when do you use AI, and for what? Strategy, execution, analysis. Strategy stays human. What matters, what bets, what you stop. AI is the sparring partner, never the author. Execution goes to agents, build the variants, draft, instrument, ship, analysis, the agent drafts the readout. A human calls it scrap or scale. Here's the anti-pattern. A direct report prompts Claude or Chach-IPT for a growth strategy, and has you a long AI written strategy doc. What do you think? That the agent is doing their thinking? That's not why you hired them. Team of one, you hold the strategy. Team of five, you write the guardrails, where AI is allowed, where it is not, and a team decides inside them. Now, the one-on-ones. Most managers run them as a status update. That's low leverage. Now an agent writes a status update before you even sit down. So the whole one-on-one goes to transfer in your judgment. So they decide well when you're not in the room. Direction, same thing. Say what matters most right now and how each role ladders up to it. Then have them play it back to you, and write the trade-offs down. Speed or rigor, polish or rough first draft, spend or protect the budget. And so do your agents. An agent only knows the trade-offs that you put in writing. Team of one, that strategy doc is the context file every agent reads. My own content operation runs on 29 agent definitions in one folder with five human gates where judgment stays with me. Team of five, that same doc keeps your people and their agents aligned. Now, scale-up mode, where testing volume used to force headcount. Play one, the experiment loop. Agents mine the recordings and the funnel for drop-off. Draft a prioritized backlog, plan the test, build the variance and the flag, and write the readout. You pick the bets and call scrap or scale. AI drafts more tests. It doesn't change the sample size a test needs. Play two, the churn agent. It watches usage and tickets. Flags who is likely to leave. Retries failed payments on the best schedule. Draft the save message. You own the template and the offer. Play three, the Monday digest. The agent reads their R dashboard, flags what moved, writes the readout. No status meeting. Play four, programmatic SEO. Agents draft acquisition pages at scale, and Google's test is of value to the user no matter how the page is made up. So a page that adds nothing stays out of the search. Team of one, that is your stack. Team of five, every play gets an owner, and the bets land on your desk. Fewer people, higher velocity. Every human hour on a call, only the human should make. And hey, click that subscribe button. And if you want to know the difference between an AI growth engineer and an AI product engineer, click right here.
